solve-ap_us_history-real_c_emanc-0.note: Lincoln explicitly invokes his power 'as Commander-in-Chief' and calls it 'a fit and necessary war measure.'
The proclamation marked the turn in Union war aims from just restoring the Union to also ending slavery.

The full proclamation allowed Black men to serve in the armed forces, and about 180,000 served in the army plus more in the navy. The border states were exempted, and Britain and France never recognized the Confederacy.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_emanc-1.note: The excerpt cites his power as Commander-in-Chief and a war measure to suppress rebellion.
The proclamation marked a shift in Union war aims from restoring the Union alone to also ending slavery.
The proclamation announced that freed men would be received into the armed services, leading to large-scale Black enlistment.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_monroe-0.note: The message warns Europe against interposing to oppress the newly independent governments. That reflects fear that the Holy Alliance would intervene to restore Spanish rule.
The excerpt says outright that the U.S. 'shall not interfere' with existing colonies but would view European oppression of the new states as unfriendly.
The context is the Latin American revolutions and the European monarchies' interest in restoring control. The other options come from later periods.
Monroe's refusal to take part in European wars continues Washington's 1793 neutrality policy and the advice in his Farewell Address.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_monroe-1.note: Monroe warned against European interposition to oppress newly independent governments, as the Holy Alliance might do.
The text says the US will not interfere with existing colonies but would view oppression of independent states as unfriendly.
The Monroe Doctrine responded to Latin American independence movements and the threat of European monarchies restoring control.
Non-involvement in European wars echoes Washington's Neutrality Proclamation and his Farewell Address advice.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_fsa-0.note: The act commanded citizens to help, kept accused fugitives from testifying, punished anyone who interfered, and paid commissioners more for ruling in the claimant's favor. All of this made recovery easier for slaveholders.
The excerpt says all good citizens are 'commanded to aid and assist,' and it sets a fine and jail time for anyone who obstructs an arrest, rescues a fugitive, helps an escape, or hides a fugitive.
The act was part of the Compromise of 1850, which tried to settle the sectional fight over slavery in land taken from Mexico.

Northern anger at the law led to personal liberty laws, more rescues of fugitives, and Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852). Congress did not repeal the law until 1864, during the war, so option 3 is wrong.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_fsa-1.note: Provisions command citizens to assist, bar fugitive testimony, penalize obstruction; all favor slaveholders.
Excerpt commands good citizens to aid and punishes aiding escape.
The act was part of the Compromise of 1850 following the Mexican Cession.
Northern backlash fueled antislavery sentiment, personal liberty laws, and Uncle Tom's Cabin.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_jones-0.note: He hopes they succeed and points them toward 'extortioners.'
Text says the few men in the crowd were foreign residents with exemptions in their pockets, and that these aliens incited the pillage.
Prices in Richmond rose because of the blockade, army demand for supplies, and Confederate paper money.

Both are anger over unfair exemptions from military service. One caveat: the Richmond complaint is about foreigners who were exempt, while the Northern anger was about the rich paying to get out of the draft (substitutes and the $300 commutation fee). Still, option 3 is clearly the closest match.

solve-ap_us_history-real_c_jones-1.note: Jones hopes they succeed and says plenty is in the hands of extortioners.
He says the men were mostly foreign residents with exemptions in their pockets, and that aliens incited pillage.
Blockade, army demand, and paper money issuance drove Confederate inflation and shortages.
Class-based resentment of exemptions parallels Northern anger at commutation and substitutes, as in the 1863 draft riots.

verdicts.note: Key is directly supported by the quoted 'interposition ... unfriendly disposition' passage; distractor rationales are accurate (Adams-Onís signed 1819, ratified 1821).
Key paraphrases the non-interference/anti-oppression distinction in the text; each distractor is contradicted by the excerpt as the rationales state.
Context of Latin American independence and Holy Alliance/French restoration of Ferdinand VII in Spain (1823) is accurate; distractors are correctly dated as anachronistic.
Neutrality Proclamation (1793) and Farewell Address (1796) are correctly described; the 'never taken any part' sentence is a clear continuity with that policy. Distractor descriptions are accurate.

Key is directly supported by the quoted 'Commander-in-Chief ... fit and necessary war measure' language; distractor rationales (no amendment until Dec. 1865, no such Supreme Court ruling, border states not a source) are accurate.

Shift in Union war aims toward emancipation is the standard context; distractor rationales are accurate (Reconstruction plans later; Lincoln pursued harder war, not negotiated peace; Fugitive Slave Act repeal not the immediate setting).

Full proclamation's armed-service clause and ~180,000 Black soldiers (plus ~19,000 sailors) are accurate; Britain and France never recognized the Confederacy; border-state slavery ended by state action/13th Amendment. Stem explicitly signals reliance on knowledge beyond the excerpt, which is acceptable for the skill.
Key is clearly supported by the quoted provisions (citizen assistance command, exclusion of fugitive testimony, penalties, $10/$5 fee differential). Distractor rationales are historically accurate.

Quoted wording matches the act (Sections 5 and 7); penalty figures ($1,000 fine, six months) are correct. Rationale for option 3 correctly notes seizure 'with or without process' (Section 6). No distractor is defensible.
Act was part of the Compromise of 1850 following the Mexican Cession; dates in distractor rationales (1787, 1820, 1860–61) are accurate.
Northern resistance, 1850s personal liberty laws, and Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) are standard effects; repeal in June 1864 is correct; the Kansas-Nebraska Act reference is accurate.

Key is directly supported by the quoted passage (hope the crowd succeeds; 'plenty in the hands of the extortioners'). Distractor rationales are accurate; Governor Letcher did call out the Public Guard, consistent with [1]'s rationale.

Key matches the text: few men, 'mostly foreign residents, with exemptions in their pockets', and exempted aliens 'incited to pillage valuables'. Campbell as Assistant Secretary of War and Meredith's ruling are historically accurate.
Blockade, army requisitions/impressment, and unbacked Confederate paper money are the standard causes of Richmond's 1863 inflation; distractors are clearly wrong.

The $300 commutation fee and substitute hiring under the 1863 Enrollment Act, and the July 1863 New York City draft riots, are accurately stated; the analogy to resentment of exemptions is apt. Other options are accurately described and clearly not parallel.
